original_question: For a compact smooth Riemannian manifold, is security equivalent to flatness? In other words, is every secure compact smooth Riemannian manifold flat, and every flat one secure?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 3 in §5.6: "A compact, smooth riemannian manifolds is secure if and only if it is flat."
correct_elements: Your draft already identifies the correct target almost exactly: it has the right ambient objects (compact smooth Riemannian manifolds), the right two properties (security and flatness), and the intended if-and-only-if form of the paper's conjecture.
missing_details: The paper's notion of security should be stated explicitly: for every pair of points x,y in the manifold, there exists a finite blocking set B contained in M \ {x,y} such that every geodesic segment joining x to y meets B.
The relevant connecting curves are geodesics (the manifold analogue of billiard orbits), not arbitrary paths.
To be fully stand-alone, the question should refer to the Riemannian metric explicitly, e.g. (M,g), since flatness is a property of the metric.
'Flat' should be clarified as Riemannian flatness, i.e. zero sectional curvature everywhere.

The nearby context first defines security for billiard tables and only then says that the same framework applies more generally to Riemannian manifolds; a stand-alone formulation should therefore carry over the blocking-set definition explicitly.
The conjecture is specifically about compact smooth Riemannian manifolds, not the broader class of manifolds with boundary, corners, or singularities mentioned in the surrounding discussion.
refined_question: Let (M,g) be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold. Call (M,g) secure if for every pair of points x,y in M there exists a finite set B ⊂ M \ {x,y} such that every geodesic segment in M joining x to y passes through at least one point of B. Is (M,g) secure if and only if g is flat, equivalently, if and only if M has zero sectional curvature everywhere?
justification: The draft is a near-verbatim paraphrase of the paper's actual target, namely Conjecture 3 in §5.6. The only real omissions are definitional: §5.6 first introduces security via finite blocking sets for pairs of points, then says that this framework extends from billiard tables to Riemannian manifolds, and immediately formulates the compact-manifold flatness conjecture. The sentence just before Conjecture 3 also records that flat manifolds are secure, so the draft has the correct scope and logical shape but needs the blocking-set definition to be fully self-contained and paper-faithful.
